webTitle: Morning Mail: Pauline Hanson’s right-hand man, warnings Moscow may target Nato, and the end of card surcharges

fields.headline: Morning Mail: Pauline Hanson’s right-hand man, warnings Moscow may target Nato, and the end of card surcharges
fields.trailText: Australians to no longer be hit with card surcharges; James Ashby’s rise in One Nation; Beijing believes AI slowdown would favour US
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Episode two of The Populist, out today, tracks the rise and influence of Pauline Hanson’s right-hand man: James Ashby. Overseas, there are warnings from intelligence chiefs that Russia may soon test the resolve of the Nato military alliance. Meanwhile, China is taking a dim view of US warnings over the breakneck speed of AI development. Australia Explainer | Debit and credit card surcharges will be eliminated from 1 October, as part of Reserve Bank reforms that will do away with extra checkout fees on Visa, Mastercard, and Eftpos payments. Exclusive | One Nation’s national director, James Ashby, is enjoying generous benefits as a result of his role working for One Nation, with documents showing that a company linked to the party built a $56,000 shed on his central Queensland property. The road ahead | Australian households will shrink but more people can expect to live well into their 90s, according to the Treasury’s latest intergenerational report looking ahead 40 years into the future. Valley Heights stabbings | A child has died in a stabbing attack in the Blue Mountains, with two other children and a woman being treated in hospital in a critical condition, NSW police say. Outfoxed? | Most people can identify wombats and kangaroos as Australian animals, but one in six people surveyed in Queensland, NSW and Victoria think red foxes are native wildlife. World Russia-Ukraine war | Baltic spy chiefs warn Moscow is preparing for more decisive action in Europe; Ukraine has targeted Moscow and the surrounding region in a large-scale attack involving hundreds of drones on the final day of Russia’s parliamentary elections. Analysis | China is pushing back against US warnings over rapid AI development, as Beijing views calls for a slowdown as a mechanism to lock in advantages enjoyed by American tech companies. Middle East crisis | Nations across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign. ‘Profound upheaval’ | Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office despite his party’s heavy losses in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party. Back on stage | Amid continued calls for a fan boycott, Ed Sheeran says the situation in Gaza is “catastrophic and unjustifiable” in his first show since his tour plunged into turmoil. Triumphal arch | Donald Trump claims the triumphal arch he is planning for Washington DC will serve as a “top grade military complex” replete with drone and ammunition storage space. Podcast The Populist: The favourite son | Episode 2 Most Australians know the story of Pauline Hanson: the fish and chip shop, the maiden speech, the “please explain”. But Hanson’s top adviser, James Ashby, wields as much – if not more – power over One Nation as Hanson herself. When the party bars media from press conferences, it’s Ashby who makes the call. To understand how One Nation operates, it’s important to understand Ashby’s story, from his beginnings as a PR flack, through a massive political scandal, to his ascent to power as One Nation’s popularity soars. In-depth The frustrations of American voters are many and varied: grifters, liars, the two-party system, money influencing elections, the US’s standing in the world, growing national debt and a fixation on cultural issues, not just the larger problems plaguing the country. Voters rage is reshaping US politics – and the looming midterms are starting to be framed not as right versus left but instead the “well-fed versus the fed-up”. Not the news It’s been a huge couple of years for Way Dynamic, the Melbourne multi-instrumentalist whose real name is Dylan Young. His 2025 album Massive Shoe is about to be re-released internationally after he signed with the indie giant Jagjaguwar. With subtle yet lush layers, gentle vocals and pensive lyricism, Way Dynamic’s thoughtful, sunny folk is both contemporary and timeless – and it’s not hard to understand his success. Sport AFL | Was Hawthorn v Brisbane the best game of Australian rules football ever played, Jonathan Horn asks. Cricket | Australia deny Zimbabwe a consolation ODI win after Nathan Ellis pulls off last-over heist in Harare; Brendon McCullum hails Harry Brook’s captaincy as England move top of T20 world rankings. Football | Alexander Isak pounces to give Liverpool victory on Iraola’s return to Bournemouth; Antoine Semenyo helps chaotic Manchester City beat Sunderland 5-3 despite Brian Brobbey hat-trick; Matheus Cunha strikes late to deny Fulham and salvage point for Manchester United. Tennis | Alex de Minaur finds top gear to seal Australia’s Davis Cup progression over Poland. Rugby union | Wallaroos give up big lead as France make miracle comeback in match delayed by burning bus. Media roundup A survey has revealed that Australians are waiting years for dementia diagnoses with early warning signs sometimes overlooked by health professionals, ABC News reports. Disposable vapes, toys, singing birthday cards and rechargeable tools are among the devices causing thousands of fires in waste and recycling centres across Australia, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. What’s happening today Politics | Treasurer Jim Chalmers is set to release the latest intergenerational report this morning. SA | A coronial inquest is scheduled in Adelaide into the death of a woman who was approved for NDIS support but did not receive care. ACT | A public hearing is scheduled in the inquiry into defence amendment (sexual assault prevention, intervention and response commission) bill. Sign up Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email If you would like to receive this Morning Mail update to your email inbox every weekday, sign up here, or finish your day with our Politics, really newsletter. You can follow the latest in US politics by signing up for This Week in Trumpland. Brain teaser And finally, here are the Guardian’s crosswords to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword

webTitle: House Republican doubles down on jab at Trump’s immigration enforcement

fields.headline: House Republican doubles down on jab at Trump’s immigration enforcement
fields.trailText: Florida’s María Elvira Salazar warns Trump that advisers are ‘compromising his legacy’ and not showing ‘whole picture’
fields.bodyText: María Elvira Salazar, the Republican congresswoman who has accused the president of going too far on immigration enforcement, doubled down on her criticism of the administration on Sunday, warning Donald Trump that some of his advisers were “compromising his legacy”. In an interview with CBS News’s Face the Nation, the Florida representative who is locked in a tight race for re-election pleaded with the US president not to “squander” his relationship with Hispanic voters. Though she couched her remarks as criticism of top administration advisers, it was clear that her focus was on Trump’s much-vaunted ambition to carry out the largest mass deportation of undocumented immigrants in US history. “I’m forewarning him and advising him as a member of Congress from the south Florida area that some of his advisers are just not presenting the whole picture,” she said. Asked by Face the Nation whether she were referring to Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, or Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff who has spearheaded the removal of undocumented children, Salazar placed the onus on Trump. “He is the only elected official in the White House. He is the one who has to determine who he listens and who he does not listen to. He is the president.” Last week Salazar became a rare voice of internal criticism within the Republican party towards Trump when she released a 30-second advert pointing out that even law-abiding undocumented immigrants were getting caught up in the aggressive federal sweep. The ad said: “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy … The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” Salazar’s warning has been backed up by a slew of recent opinion polls that show many Hispanic voters who helped re-elect Trump in 2024 are now turning away from him. They are being repulsed by the rising cost of living and concern about his handling of the economy, as well as by the hardline immigration drive that has led to many hardworking, taxpaying undocumented immigrants being rounded up, detained and deported. In her CBS News interview, Salazar described herself as “a proud Republican”. “I’m first-generation American, and I want to preserve the American values that are entrenched in the [Republican party] and that the Hispanics share”. She is currently facing a tough re-election battle in her Miami-area district against her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, despite having won in 2024 by 20 points. Trump also won the district by 15 points that year. Salazar told CBS News that 70% of Americans wanted to see some type of immigration reform. She also pushed back on the administration’s deportation of all undocumented immigrants irrespective of their criminal status. “The average America understands the difference between the narco and the nanny, and the gangster and the gardener.” On Saturday, Trump responded to Salazar’s criticisms, saying: “She obviously doesn’t have a very strong feeling about the border. I do.” He added: “Without me, she wouldn’t have gotten elected.” By breaking her silence on immigration, Salazar has put a spotlight on rising fears within Republican circles that the displeasure of Hispanic voters towards the administration’s policies could cost the party dear in November’s midterm elections. Several House seats in Colorado, Florida, Texas, Nevada and other states could be tipped in the Democrats’ favor as a result. Steve Scalise, the second-most powerful Republican in the US House, acknowledged on ABC News’s This Week that immigration was creating divisions within his party. Asked what he thought of Salazar’s comment that many Hispanic voters feel betrayed, he said: “I don’t necessarily agree with that statement.” He added: “When you look at what María said, obviously we have a lot of disagreements in Congress … Even among Republicans we have disagreements on how to actually get to the secure border that we have.”

webTitle: ‘I don’t trust him any more’: Pennsylvanians come to grips with John Fetterman’s rightwing turn

fields.headline: ‘I don’t trust him any more’: Pennsylvanians come to grips with John Fetterman’s rightwing turn
fields.trailText: The maverick senator has isolated himself from supporters as he has become a strident supporter of Israel
fields.bodyText: Two eras, two videos, shot against the same physical backdrop, convey political messages that seem a world removed from each other. The contrasting films, produced eight years apart, neatly distill the evolution of John Fetterman, Pennsylvania’s maverick senator in his journey from progressive icon to a man seemingly more at ease with his nominal Republican opponents than his fellow Democrats. Fetterman’s evolution has been so stark that some Democrats fear he will go over to the Republicans – jeopardizing the party’s hopes of regaining control of the Senate – despite his disavowals of such intentions. Longtime activists say his stock within the party has dropped to the point where his chances of being re-elected as a Democrat are zero. A 2018 video for Fetterman’s successful campaign to be the state’s lieutenant governor opens with footage of Braddock, Pennsylvania’s landmark Mon Valley Edgar Thomson steelworks to the soundtrack of Donald Trump condemning previous US presidents for allowing industrial jobs to disappear and vowing that only he could bring them back. “Donald Trump hasn’t shown up since then, and he won’t because he never cared about places like this,” Fetterman says on camera, accusing Trump of using towns like Braddock as a prop. Braddock, a down-at-the-heel town of fewer than 2,000 residents on the Monongahela River near Pittsburgh, seemed emblematic of the left-behind communities Trump had wooed as he ran for president with promises to revive hollowed-out industries and restore lost jobs. It is also where Fetterman, a mayor for more than decade, cut his teeth as a highly unorthodox politician who broke with convention to attract investment to a shattered local economy and kickstart community projects, sometimes with his own money. His no-holds-barred approach combined with his trademark dress of shorts and hoodie once earned him the moniker of “America’s coolest mayor”. Braddock’s giant steel plant, which has dominated the local landscape since 1875, was the first in the US to be established by the steel magnate and philanthropist Andrew Carnegie, and is core to the town’s identity as a once thriving working-class hub now scarred by neglect. But this month, Fetterman used it as a setting for another video – this time aimed at Republicans in their midterm convention gathering in Dallas and signaling solidarity with Trump. “I’m a commonsense Democrat,” he proclaimed in a recorded message introducing his fellow Pennsylvania senator, Dave McCormick, a Republican and loyal Trump acolyte with whom he has forged a close bond. “I’m always trying to reject the extremes in socialism and that anti-American way of life. “Dave McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done. Right back over my shoulder, that’s the iconic US Steel mill, and that’s exactly the kind of thing that will work together and will work with President Trump to fight and defend the steel way of life right here in the steel valley.” The video was greeted with rapturous applause by Republicans, gathered at Trump’s behest to mobilize enthusiasm for November’s midterm elections amid sagging poll numbers. But for Democrats, Fetterman’s incongruous appearance may be the last straw in a series of perceived betrayals that have fueled a clamor to block his bid to run for re-election in 2028, when his Senate seat is up for grabs. “What happened to the guy that beat up on Donald Trump in 2018 because he didn’t care?” said Mike Sturla, who served as Democratic state legislator from Lancaster for 34 years and staged a fundraising dinner for Fetterman’s 2022 Senate run after being captivated by his earlier campaign video and subsequent performance as lieutenant governor. “Trump was still popular at the time and people were reluctant to attack him. So I was really impressed. I was like, ‘Good lord! Finally, somebody’s willing to just stand up and punch the guy on the nose.’” By contrast, Fetterman’s latest video, argued Sturla, created “the perception that he’s complicit” with the Republicans. Cries of disloyalty have steadily increased since Fetterman took his Senate seat in 2023, seven months after suffering a debilitating stroke while campaigning in Lancaster that left with him acute speech and communication challenges. He later underwent treatment for clinical depression, a common post-stroke condition. Criticism has intensified since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, with Fetterman repeatedly praising the US president’s protectionist policies and appeal to working-class voters. While most Democrats recoiled at Trump’s second presidential victory, Fetterman took steps to mollify the man he had once vilified, visiting him at Mar-a-Lago days before the inauguration. Since then, Fetterman has gained a high profile as a strident advocate for Israel, defending it from charges of genocide in Gaza even as fellow Democrats openly criticize or distance themselves from the country. Fetterman’s changing political profile has coincided with allegations that he has shown scant interest in doing his job as a senator. The Wall Street Journal reported that he had declined to meet a group of paralyzed military veterans to discuss legislation that could help their care, citing illness, yet was well enough on the same day to keep an appointment with Fox News to discuss Israel and the war with Iran. (The Guardian contacted Fetterman’s office.) He has also refused to meet officials from the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia to discuss Medicaid cuts, according to the newspaper. In the Senate, Fetterman is said to have avoided close ties to fellow Democrats while striking up friendships with Republicans, such as McCormick and Katie Britt, a conservative senator from Alabama. It is a far cry from his spell as Braddock’s mayor, and Sturla said it also contrasted with Fetterman’s time as Pennsylvania’s lieutenant governor, when he visited each of the state’s 67 counties in a controversial campaign to legalize marijuana, a cause which enamored him to liberal-minded progressives and gave him a statewide platform to launch his Senate campaign. Lynn Miller, a longtime Democratic activist who was Fetterman’s de facto campaign manager in Lancaster county during his Senate campaign, said he triumphed in a primary over Conor Lamb, a Democratic representative who was seen as an establishment candidate, because he appeared to be progressive and “different”. “I liked everything I heard,” said Miller, who recalls waiting to introduce Fetterman to an expectant audience at Millersville University, near Lancaster, only for the event to be canceled at the last moment. She later learned that he had suffered a stoke. “He really emphasized that he was different, that he wasn’t a typical politician, and that just appealed.” Miller now professes herself to be “disappointed” and is demanding the return of her campaign donations. “His alliance at times with President Trump is unforgivable,” she said. “He says he’s a commonsense Democrat. Well, dude, that’s not how you sold yourself five years ago. “I’ve put together the list of all the campaign contributions that I’ve made, and tried emailing addresses that I’ve been given. I want my donations back.” Yet in Braddock, where Fetterman still lives, residual loyalty endures. Residents and local business people insist that Fetterman – who sports a tattoo of the town’s zip code, 15104, and of the dates of murders that happened on his watch – remains unchanged. Some cite the Braddock Free Store, set up and run by Fetterman’s wife, Gisele, to give away donated goods free of charge, as an example of the public-spiritedness the couple bring to community. The makeshift facility is emblazoned with messages of peace and harmony that are replicated throughout the town center – and which contrast with the blighted environment, in the form of grandiose but derelict buildings and empty lots. Approached at the store on Braddock Avenue, the town’s main thoroughfare, Gisele Fetterman declined to be interviewed, adding that her husband was in Washington. Speculation has swirled about the state of the couple’s marriage, with some noting Gisele’s reduced profile after having previously played a critical role in her husband’s campaigning. “I really liked how he deferred to Gisele. I liked the role that she was playing,” said Miller. “But she has like disappeared from social media. She used to have a huge presence on social media promoting him, things about the family, etc.” But Cheryl Johnson, who runs Aunt Cheryl’s Cafe in a community center building that Fetterman helped to purchase with $50,000 of his own funds, said the senator was being harshly criticized for bipartisan cooperation that would have been considered normal in a less-polarized era. “Some of the things Senator Fetterman has done, I think at another time would not have been criticized as much,” Johnson argued. “What has he done that has hurt the Democrats? He and McCormick are the two senators from the state of Pennsylvania. There was a time where you knew politicians went across the aisle. “He has never been a cookie-cutter kind of guy. We knew he was different from the beginning, the way he presented himself – for instance, in fashion and how he dressed. He never cared if he offended people. “But some of the things he and his wife have done for this community have been great. The fact that he would even come to a community like this says something.” Al Boss, who runs a local optician’s office, fondly recalled Fetterman using the bulk of his 6ft 8in, 325lb frame to single-handedly rescue his car after it got stuck in a winter snow storm. “I was driving a little Mercedes sports car and had got trapped in a snow drift,” said Boss, 76. “He practically lifted the backside of the car up and pulled me out of the snow. I don’t even think he was mayor then.” Yet Fetterman’s altered political profile has not gone unnoticed. Chris Baldy, 63, a materials chemist from Pittsburgh visiting Boss’s optician’s shop, said he had been “pleasantly surprised” that Fetterman’s Senate performance had chimed with his own Republican sympathies. “When he was coming in, knowing this area and what he had done here, I was concerned that he was very far left,” said Baldy. “Now I see what he is doing is more what I would consider to be common sense.” Jeanette, 68, a retired nurse who declined to give her last name, said she had moved to Braddock after being attracted by its newly built apartment blocks and the reputation that Fetterman’s actions as mayor had generated. But the move had turned sour and Fetterman was no longer visibly present in the community. “This is not a good place. I want to leave,” she said, citing night-time crime, drug-taking and urgent home repairs that go unattended. Referring to Fetterman, she added: “I don’t trust him any more. I used to like him and talk with him. You would see him every other day when he was trying to get elected. Now I haven’t seen him for a whole year, maybe two.” Officials on the Allegheny country Democratic committee, which covers Braddock, did not respond to requests for comments. Members of the Braddock borough council and the state representative for the area, Abigail Salisbury, also did not respond after the Guardian visited their offices. Analysts say such reticence may be partly caused by a wariness of driving Fetterman into defecting to the Republicans, a move that could stymie Democratic hopes of recapturing control of the Senate after November’s midterms. Fetterman has previously said he would only abandon the Democrats if they became “the anti-Israel party”. But Mike Weidinger, a veteran activist in GOP-dominated Lancaster county with extensive state wide connections, wrote off Fetterman’s re-election chances when his seat comes up for grabs in 2028. “He’ll never be elected again in this state as a Democrat,” Weidinger declared. If he wants to run for the Senate again, he will be primaried and he will lose. “Among Democrat activists he’s toast as a Democrat. I think that’s a pretty common opinion across the state.”

webTitle: ‘People are pissed off’: anger at the elite and the establishment is fueling this year’s midterms

fields.headline: ‘People are pissed off’: anger at the elite and the establishment is fueling this year’s midterms
fields.trailText: Coming midterm elections are starting to be framed not as right versus left but instead the ‘well-fed versus the fed-up’
fields.bodyText: Brian Leeland, a 79-year-old Democratic voter in Detroit, had enough. Frustrated by the way the US media covers this febrile political era, from Donald Trump’s Washington to political campaigns across the country, he contacted the Guardian. “Your decision to frame the race here as a simple progressive versus establishment choice is overly simplistic verging on lazy,” he wrote to this reporter, after our coverage of progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign in the Democratic US Senate primary in Michigan. “As an electorate, we are not binary for the convenience of the media.” His was a complaint I heard often as I traveled across the midwest to cover a host of contested Democratic primaries. So I called him up. Leeland’s list of frustrations is long: grifters, liars, the two-party system, money influencing elections, the US’s standing in the world, the growing national debt and a fixation on cultural issues, not just the larger problems that plague the country. He is one of many angry voters whose rage is reshaping American politics. It could decide the balance of power in Washington this November and stymie the president’s final years in office – and help determine what comes next for the left after Trump. Headlines from this year’s midterm primaries have ping-ponged back and forth – between major wins for progressives and moderates in Democratic races, defeats and victories for big money, and tests of Trump’s power over the Republican party. But on the campaign trail in contested Democratic primaries throughout the midwest, I found that attempts to tease out ideological trend lines obscured a deeper reality. More than any factional battle between one wing of a party over another, this year’s midterm primary elections is punctuated by a profound dissatisfaction with the political status quo. American voters are mad – at pretty much everything. I live in Minneapolis, and the anger at the Trump administration over Operation Metro Surge and the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti still dominates most political conversations many months later. In Michigan, multiple people described themselves to me as more moderate, then railed against the status quo. At a coffee shop near the Canadian border, a man emotionally injected himself into my conversation with a local leader to say how upset Canadians are. Voters can’t afford healthcare or childcare. Grocery and gas prices keep rising while the richest people keep lining their pockets. Farmers and small business owners are contending with tariffs and a trade war. Small town residents are beating back datacenters and tearing down Flock cameras. They don’t want the US to be involved in wars overseas. Women’s rights and access to abortion care are on a backslide. A “pissed-off majority” is finding its voice, according to Maurice Mitchell, the national director of the Working Families party, a progressive third political party that’s seen its endorsees winning bigger than ever this year. “Most people around the country, many of whom don’t even identify as Democrat or Republican or whatever, are 10 out of 10 pissed off, angry and willing to take that anger into action against the status quo.” Trump, of course, himself rode a wave of voter anger at the political establishment – both in 2016 and again in 2024. He sought to stir up anger at his enemies, immigrants, trans people, the so-called “deep state”. But in his second term – with material conditions deteriorating for many Americans as wealth accumulates at the top, disruption caused by the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence, an unsanctioned war in Iran, failed accountability on the Epstein files and trade wars with friendly nations – Trump is now a target of the very anti-establishment anger he stoked. Trump’s political project has sought to harness anger and apportion blame. The administration’s common argument that the reason people can’t get well-paying jobs is because of immigrants is a central example, said Anat Shenker-Osorio, a progressive political consultant. It’s a common story that authoritarians tell – that “those people” are standing in the way, she said. But Mitchell, of the Working Families party, said this scapegoating playbook is falling flat after a decade. “If you’re claiming that the source of my pain [is] trans people and DEI and immigrants, and now you have the ball and you’ve used that power to make those people’s lives hell, but my life isn’t better, then the jig is up,” he said. Who’s left to punch down at? Democrats relied on disgust at Trump to carry them to victory in 2020. But this election year, voters are asking for more. The candidates who have run on that hunger for a different vision of politics have been rewarded by voters in their party’s primaries. Rob Sand, the Democratic contender for the Iowa governor’s seat, regularly calls out the two-party system. He has framed his quest to win over red-state voters not as left versus right, but “well-fed versus the fed-up”. Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee for a US Senate seat in Florida, and a democratic socialist, said voters have not cared about any intraparty label. They care more that she cares about people, she suggested. “I’m actually going to look out for just regular, everyday people and put them first and put forth policies that will positively impact them,” she said. “And so, yeah, I’m getting hit from all different sides, but I know I’m on the right side of history because I’m resonating with people, and they’re realizing that in the next 250 years, what’s been happening doesn’t have to continue to happen.” The final test in November, however, will reveal if their message resonates across the board, with voters of all political backgrounds. “They want to see you fighting for the things you said you would fight for, and doing the things you said you would do,” said El-Sayed. “And too often, the very people who tell them they’re fighting for them turn around and do the same exact thing that they swore they’d never do.” *** The laundry list of issues enraging voters is long – so long, in fact, it can be harder to find areas in which people think the country is headed in the right direction than spots where there is broad dissatisfaction. Phil Verges, a 65-year-old farmer from Spring Valley, Wisconsin, recently became old enough to qualify for Medicare. As a farmer, he struggled with healthcare costs much of his life, as he watched his parents do for much of theirs. While he’s glad to have the coverage, the whole thing has been “bittersweet”. He recalled being in his 20s and thinking that by the time he would be old enough for Medicare there would be some kind of universal coverage in the US. “So that hit me kind of hard,” Verges. “Four decades have gone by and we’re still not doing the right thing, at least in my opinion, with healthcare.” The US is the only nation with GoFundMe campaigns for hospital bills – or before that, a spaghetti dinner to raise funds in small towns like his, he said. “People are getting sick and tired of being sick and tired,” Verges said. Sarah Agnew, a 56-year-old Democrat in Minnesota, said her party hasn’t done enough to stand up to Trump. But she has faith in some candidates this year who she really believes in, including the Minnesota US Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan and the Texas US Senate candidate James Talarico. For her, accountability for the Trump administration is most critical right now. “I want to see accountability for Alex Pretti and Renee Good, and I want to see accountability for Kristi Noem and everybody who is responsible for what happened here in our state and our city,” she said. Milan van Dam, the 17-year-old national chair of the High School Democrats of America, will be just shy of voting age this November. He was in second grade when Trump was elected. Trump has always been part of politics for him, but he and other young voters aren’t craving a return to the pre-Trump status quo they never knew. They want something better. It’s not that all young people are suddenly interested in socialism, he said, a common diagnosis from political pundits: they just don’t accept an incremental approach to politics. “The vast majority of people voting for these candidates, who in some cases happen to be democratic socialists, aren’t democratic socialists.” The mounting sentiment against the system has been building since at least the 2008 recession, when voters felt the government did not do enough to help everyday people while banks and big businesses got bailed out, according to AJ Simmons, research director of the Center for State Policy and Leadership at the University of Illinois Springfield. National elections have vacillated back and forth between the two major parties, but many of the Americans who voted for them have concluded that neither can actually fix the underlying problems. At a time when it feels as if the country is in freefall, Simmons suggested many of its citizens are craving both authenticity and competence. “People are getting [to] a point of ‘I don’t know how much I care about the culture war – I can’t eat blueberries, I can’t eat lettuce, I can’t get healthcare. Will you do one of those things?’” he said. *** Seth Bodnar, an independent running for US Senate in Montana, shot a Flock camera with a gun in a recent campaign ad that railed against the mass surveillance, saying big tech was using them to track “our every move” then storing the data in datacenters they want to build “in our back yards”. “They are all getting rich and we’re getting screwed, and nobody is holding them accountable,” Bodnar said, as Trump simultaneously spent the week advocating for unfettered growth of the tech sector. The current crop of candidates challenging the status quo are running on “solidarity populism”, Mitchell said – giving voice to the anger and calling out the villains who deserve to see it directed at them, instead of blaming people who don’t have power. Flanagan, the Minnesota US Senate candidate, said one of the things Trump did well was to talk about how the economy was rigged. What’s become clearer, as Trump built a gilded ballroom and billionaires lined their pockets, she said, was that the president and his friends were the ones doing the rigging. The rage is even more crystalized when the impact is felt close to home. Flanagan went to the iconic Minnesota state fair on opening day. Imagery of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown dominated the artwork made of locally grown seeds and plants – a sign, she said, that the state’s voters have not moved on from the trauma and disruption caused by Operation Metro Surge. “Folks have had it, and they want people who are going to push back,” she said. At a county fair last month, Rebecca Cooke, the Wisconsin congressional hopeful, said she had spoken to a man who told her he had voted for her opponent, Republican Derrick Van Orden, twice, but wouldn’t be doing so again because of “this goddamn war”. Cooke wants to point such anger and ire at the ultra-wealthy, the tech billionaires, the people making record profits off American workers. In Ohio, Nan Whaley, the 2022 Democratic contender for governor, had beers in recent days with a former Republican turned independent. The voter was worked up, she said, about healthcare costs, rising government debt and billionaires like Elon Musk not paying their fair share of taxes. Whaley said she hears other complaints from young people about the quality of available jobs and the affordability of raising kids. A cab driver recently told her he had voted for Trump, she said, but didn’t realize the president was “going to steal everything that wasn’t nailed down”. “People are very, very angry that there have been people in office that are viewed as the establishment and nobody seems to care about the problems they’re having in their daily lives,” Whaley said. William Lawrence, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s seventh congressional district, said the first step to dealing with voter anger is acknowledging and affirming it. He’s 36, and has spent his entire life seeing aspects of the American dream diminish. “People are pissed off and incredulous that our leaders could have allowed it to get this bad,” he said. “It’s Republicans and Democrats, independents and those who don’t even know what to call themselves any more, because they’re just so fed up with it.” But his goal is to make sure they don’t drop out of the political process altogether. *** The mad-as-hell faction will decide the midterms, as it often does, Shenker-Osorio said, and that is a “plague on both your houses” vote, not an embrace of Democrats. The scale of this phenomenon later this year will depend on whether enough voters view the election as marquee enough for them to turn out. “There could be a not merely blue wave, but a blue tsunami,” she said. Stephanie Matejka, a 46-year-old insurance agent in Lincoln, Nebraska, first got involved in politics during Bernie Sanders’ presidential run. She finally saw someone who she felt was speaking to issues that matters to her as a single mom. She now volunteers with the local Democrats, and thinks deep red Nebraska could elect Democrats to Congress and the governor’s office, and an independent to the US Senate, this year. As she’s driven through Nebraska, she can tell which communities saw their schools closed, consolidated into other towns’, because the small towns wither. They have to drive 100 miles (160km) away to see their grandma in a nursing home because it was the closest option. They’re contending with gas prices that make the driving even harder. “I think that’s what’s really happening is the current administration, both statewide in Nebraska and countrywide, they do not care about people’s quality of life as long as it fits their pocketbook,” she said. “And people hate that. They’re resentful of it.” Whatever happens, governing is much harder than campaigning, Simmons said. “It’s really effective to be a challenger,” he said. “It’s real hard to govern right now because you also look at Congress and how conflictual that is, how non-governing Congress is. And nobody seems to be really solving anything.” Democratic candidates insist they can work in a divided government – potentially controlling Congress, if not the White House – to build consensus positions using an “inside-outside” strategy to engage voters in pushing for positions outside the government while they advocate for them inside. But they’ll have to reckon first with their own mistakes, including their subservience to big-money donors and an often poorly articulated vision of what the party stands for, especially during the age of Trump. “Things are going to get worse before they get better, because the imbalance of power right now is so severe,” Lawrence said. “After the damage that’s been done, it’s going to be a long road back.” Leeland, the Michigan voter who emailed the Guardian, is tired of a system he believes is failing people. But he’s hoping there is a different road ahead. A generation ago, when the Republican president Ronald Reagan was in power, “I was never this angry about it”, he said. “I didn’t like it much, but I wasn’t angry about it.”

webTitle: Leftists make waves and Trump flexes muscles: US primary season takeaways

fields.headline: Leftists make waves and Trump flexes muscles: US primary season takeaways
fields.trailText: Candidates have been selected for November’s midterms – have Republicans and Democrats made the right choices?
fields.bodyText: Primary season has officially concluded in the United States, with Democrats leading the polls among voters amid widespread economic anxieties, a war with Iran and Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda continuing into the end of the year. Democratic and Republican voters have selected contenders for key races in the 3 November midterms that will decide the balance of power in Congress, and the future of both parties. Democrats have been rocked by the primary victories of leftwing candidates. Republicans have doubled down on backing the president’s policies, despite his low approval ratings. And both parties are navigating the fallout from a series of scandals that have forced some candidates from the race, while others decided to press on. Here’s a look back at what we learned over the past six months of primaries: Lawmakers fled the House in droves, ensuring a reshaped Congress in 2027 Viewed as the chamber of Congress most likely to change hands in the midterms, the House saw significant turnover this cycle, with 74 members departing, the most since 1992, according to a tally from the Pew Research Center. Some outgoing lawmakers retired, while others ran for other offices, but generally didn’t fare particularly well – only 13 made it through primaries for governorships, the Senate or other offices, with the remaining 15 were rejected by voters. Among representatives who sought re-election to the House, 11 lost their primaries, the second-highest total since 2022. Seven of these were Democrats, two of whom – Julie Johnson and Al Green – were unseated by other Democratic incumbents after they were redistricted by Texas Republicans to compete against each other. Leftists, especially Democratic socialists, rocked the party ... Of the five House Democrats who lost their primaries to newcomers, four were booted by leftist candidates with ties to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). In New York, Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair Adriano Espaillat fell to DSA member Darializa Avila Chevalier and congressman Dan Goldman was ousted by former DSA member Brad Lander, while DSA member Claire Valdez also won the primary to replace retiring congresswoman Nydia Velazquez. In Colorado, DSA member Melat Kiros unseated 30-year incumbent Diana DeGette, and in Michigan, the DSA-endorsed Donovan McKinney beat congressman Shri Thanedar. All are expected to win their seats in the midterms, as their districts are heavily Democratic. “A lot of people were hoping that it was a blip, like oh well, this is a special case,” said the DSA-endorsed Chris Rabb, who is expected to be elected to the House after winning the Democratic primary in deep-blue Philadelphia. “We showed them a different way. So I think all of those things make this election cycle uniquely powerful in ways that most people could not anticipate, myself included.” The fifth sitting Democrat to lose renomination was John Larson. His challenger, Luke Bronin, 47, successfully argued to voters that it was time to replace the 78-year-old incumbent with a younger candidate. ... but centrists are on the frontlines The battle for the House will not be decided in safe blue seats, but rather the 21 districts that the Cook Political Report considers to be toss-ups. In those districts, the nominees are almost entirely backed by the Pacs of either the center-left New Democrat Coalition, or the moderate Blue Dogs, which centrists say bolsters their arguments that their policies most closely align with the voters who determine control of Congress. “If Democrats are to win the majority in the House and/or the Senate, it will be because moderates flip seats from red to blue,” said Matt Bennett, an executive vice-president at the thinktank Third Way. There are exceptions to the trend: former DSA member William Lawrence won the Democratic nomination to take on Republican incumbent Tom Barrett in a swing Michigan congressional district, while in that state’s Democratic Senate primary, Abdul El-Sayed beat congresswoman Haley Stevens, who was backed by much of the party establishment. Anti-incumbent sentiment among Democrats had its limits The DSA’s wins reintensified debate among Democrats over the political direction of the party, but the left-wing movement’s momentum was not absolute. In Missouri, DSA member Cori Bush failed in her primary challenge against congressman Wesley Bell, who had unseated her two years ago. Hawaii congressman Ed Case fended off state senator Jarrett Keohokalole, who had challenged him from the left and argued it was time for generational change. In Massachusetts, congressman Seth Moulton made a similar argument about the Democratic senator Ed Markey, though in this case Moulton was the moderate candidate and Markey the progressive. It didn’t work, and Markey won renomination, as did other congressional Democrats in the state who faced primary challenges. In Colorado, state senator Julie Gonzales mounted an unsuccessful left-wing challenge to Democratic US senator John Hickenlooper, while in Washington, moderate congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez again won the Democratic nomination in her right-leaning district against several challengers. Trump flexed his muscles, with much success As always, Trump sought to play kingmaker in the primaries, endorsing candidates who hewed to his agenda and seeking revenge against those who had broken with him, however small their transgressions. Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie lost his primary after the president campaigned against him, and the president’s decision not to make an endorsement in Texas representative Dan Crenshaw’s primary was likely a factor in him losing the Republican nomination. Trump successfully ousted Louisiana senator Bill Cassidy – who voted to convict him after January 6 – as well as Texas senator John Cornyn, for comparatively murkier reasons. The president may rue the latter decision – recent polls have shown the Democratic nominee James Talarico with a slight lead over Trump’s preferred candidate, Ken Paxton. All told, it was a successful primary for Trump – an analysis of his record by USA Today shows nearly 97% of the candidates he backed in congressional and gubernatorial races won their primaries. There were a handful of misses – five gubernatorial candidates won their primaries without Trump’s endorsement, along with four House aspirants. Aipac spent, for better or worse The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) waded into some primaries at a particularly fraught moment for supporters of the Middle Eastern ally. Surveys show that some Republicans and many Democrats now hold negative views of Israel, amid accusations it carried out a genocide in Gaza, and many of the left-wing candidates who ousted Democratic House incumbents did so after attacking their ties to Aipac. Through its United Democracy Project Super Pac, the group nonetheless scored some wins, including Ed Gallrein’s defeat of Massie in Kentucky, Adrian Boafo’s victory in the Maryland primary to replace veteran House Democrat Steny Hoyer, and Bell’s defense against Bush’s primary challenge in Missouri. But the group failed to keep El-Sayed from defeating Rogers in the Michigan Senate primary, despite spending more than $30m in that race, or prevent progressive Aisha Wahab from winning a special election to replace former congressman Eric Swalwell in California. Some candidates fell to scandals, others pressed on Several candidates who ran for office were derailed by scandals. Graham Platner won the Democratic primary to take on veteran Republican senator Susan Collins in Maine, but dropped out amid accusations of sexual assault and misconduct. Swalwell ran for governor of California but exited that race and resigned his US House seat after he, too, was accused of sexual assault. North Carolina Republican congressman Chuck Edwards won his primary but ended his re-election campaign after the House ethics committee said he likely broke rules against sexual harassment, but Republican congressman Max Miller remains in the race amid accusations of domestic violence against his ex-wife. In other instances, the GOP used the primaries to dispose of problematic lawmakers in their ranks. Andy Ogles, a congressman with a history of homophobic and Islamophobic statements, lost in Tennessee after the Republican governor endorsed his challenger and a Super Pac backed by the renewable energy industry spent against him, and scandal-plagued congressman Cory Mills was defeated after other Florida Republicans endorsed his challenger.
